## Case study: *Araptus attenuatus*

The same analysis applies to field data, with two additions that real
samples need: tests are run within each connected component, against a
hypothesis of direction stated in advance, and the directional isolation
comparison is calibrated for the sampling design.

Garrick et al. (2013) inferred two range expansions of the peninsular lineage
of the bark beetle *Araptus attenuatus* out of a Pleistocene refugium near
27.5°N on the Baja California peninsula: a central group of populations
expanding south and a northern group expanding north.  If so, populations near
the refugium should read as sources and those farther from it as sinks, and
genetic distance should accumulate more slowly moving away from the refugium
than toward it.

### One graph, several components

The Population Graph is estimated from all peninsular sites with at least four
beetles; `decorate = TRUE` adds each site's mean coordinates to its node.

```{r arapat-graph}
#| cache: true
#| warning: false
data( arapat )

peninsula <- arapat |>
  filter( Species == "Peninsula" ) |>
  group_by( Population ) |>
  filter( n() >= 4 ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  droplevels()

beetles <- peninsula |>
  population_graph( decorate = TRUE )

beetles

igraph::components( beetles )$csize
```

The components recapitulate the regional populations of Garrick et al.
(2013): a central group, a northern group, and two southern dyads, which carry
no directional information.

### Mapping the surface on land {#sec-gravity-map}

At the degree-neutral bandwidth, `plot()` draws the gravity field at the
sites' coordinates, which `decorate = TRUE` stored in the graph.  The
source-sink scores are interpolated onto a raster, and two choices decide how
that raster appears: where it is cropped, and whether the Population Graph is
drawn over it.

The base map is a grey outline of the land from Natural Earth
(`rnaturalearth`).  The 1:10m coastline (`scale = "large"`) resolves the
islands and lagoons; it comes from `rnaturalearthhires`, which is installed
from <https://ropensci.r-universe.dev>, and `scale = "medium"` needs only
`rnaturalearthdata`.

```{r arapat-land}
#| message: false
countries <- c( "Mexico", "United States of America" )

land <- rnaturalearth::ne_countries( country = countries,
                                     scale = "large",
                                     returnclass = "sf" )

land_map <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf( data = land,
           fill = "grey85",
           colour = "grey60",
           linewidth = 0.15 ) +
  coord_sf( xlim = c( -115, -110.3 ),
            ylim = c( 24.4, 29.8 ),
            expand = FALSE ) +
  labs( x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude" ) +
  theme_bw()
```

Both southern dyads have $S = 0$ by symmetry, so only the two larger
components are mapped.  $S$ is computed within each component, so leaving the
dyads out does not change the other scores.

```{r arapat-mapped}
parts  <- igraph::components( beetles )
mapped <- beetles |>
  igraph::induced_subgraph( which( parts$csize[parts$membership] > 2 ) )

group <- igraph::components( mapped )$membership
igraph::V( mapped )$Component <- c( "Central", "Northern" )[group]

beetle_field <- mapped |>
  gravity_field()
```

#### With the topology

By default the graph is drawn over the surface.  `clip_to_base = TRUE` crops
the raster to the polygons of the base map, and `grid_n = 400` makes it fine
enough to follow the coastline.  The site labels are added with `ggrepel`, at
the node positions returned by `plot_nodes()`, because the central sites are
close together.

```{r arapat-field}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Source-sink surface of *Araptus attenuatus*, cropped to land, with the Population Graph drawn over it.  Red, source; blue, sink.  Arrows point from source to sink, with length proportional to $|\\Delta|$.  The heavy grey line is where the surfaces of the two components meet, and the dashed line is the hypothesized refugium."
#| message: false
refuge <- list(
  geom_hline( yintercept = 27.5,
              linetype = "dashed",
              colour = "grey20" ),
  annotate( "text",
            x = -110.4,
            y = 27.62,
            label = "refuge, 27.5°N",
            hjust = 1,
            size = 3.2,
            colour = "grey20" )
)

with_graph <- beetle_field |>
  plot( base = land_map,
        clip_to_base = TRUE,
        grid_n = 400,
        node_fill = "Component",
        node_labels = "none",
        subtitle_stats = FALSE )

with_graph +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel( data = plot_nodes( with_graph ),
                            aes( x, y, label = node ),
                            size = 2.7,
                            fontface = "bold",
                            point.size = 7,
                            box.padding = 0.4,
                            min.segment.length = 0.3,
                            max.overlaps = Inf,
                            bg.colour = "white",
                            bg.r = 0.12,
                            seed = 1,
                            inherit.aes = FALSE ) +
  scale_colour_manual( name = "Component",
                       values = c( Central = "#440154",
                                   Northern = "#35b779" ) ) +
  refuge
```

Because $S$ sums to zero within a component, each component is interpolated
from its own sites, and colours on the two sides of the grey boundary line are
not comparable.  `boundary = FALSE` leaves the line out.

#### Without the topology

`show_graph = FALSE` leaves out the edges, arrows, nodes and labels.  The
surface, its contours and the boundary are exactly the same, on the same colour
scale, and nothing hides the gradient:

```{r arapat-surface}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "The same surface without the topology (`show_graph = FALSE`)."
#| message: false
beetle_field |>
  plot( base = land_map,
        clip_to_base = TRUE,
        grid_n = 400,
        show_graph = FALSE,
        subtitle_stats = FALSE ) +
  refuge
```

Between the two, `graph_alpha` fades the graph rather than removing it, as a
whole (`graph_alpha = 0.35`) or by part
(`graph_alpha = c( nodes = 0.5, edges = 0.35, arrows = 0 )`).

#### The cropped raster

Cropping happens in two steps.  First, the surface of each component fills the
convex hull of its sites plus a margin (`mask = "hull"`, the default;
`mask_dist` sets the margin).  A hull drawn around sites
on a narrow peninsula crosses open water, so the second step keeps only the
cells on land.  `gravity_surface()` returns the raster itself, and its `clip`
argument takes the land polygons directly; as a data frame the two steps can be
compared side by side:

```{r arapat-crop}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| fig-cap: "The surface over each component's hull (left) and cropped to land (right)."
hull <- beetle_field |>
  gravity_surface( grid_n = 400 )

on_land <- beetle_field |>
  gravity_surface( grid_n = 400, clip = land )

hull$Area    <- "Component hulls"
on_land$Area <- "Cropped to land"

S_max <- max( abs( beetle_field$nodes$S ) )  # the limits plot() uses

land_map +
  geom_raster( aes( x, y, fill = S ),
               data = rbind( hull, on_land ),
               na.rm = TRUE ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ Area ) +
  scale_x_continuous( breaks = -114:-111 ) +
  scale_fill_gradient2( low = "#2166ac",
                        mid = "#f7f7f7",
                        high = "#b2182b",
                        limits = c( -S_max, S_max ),
                        na.value = NA )
```

With `output = "raster"` the result is a `terra` raster, with blank cells where
the surface was cropped, ready for a GIS:

```{r arapat-raster}
S_land <- beetle_field |>
  gravity_surface( grid_n = 400, clip = land, output = "raster" )
S_land
```

```{r arapat-write}
#| eval: false
terra::writeRaster( S_land, "arapat_S.tif" )
```

The Visualization chapter (@sec-visualization) builds a fuller base map with
labels and a north arrow, and @sec-gravity-3d renders this surface in relief.

### The axis: distance from the refugium

Position along the peninsula is the first principal axis of the site
coordinates (in km), and each site's distance from the refugium, $d_i$, is
measured along it.  A pair of sites is *forward* when $j$ lies farther from the
refugium than $i$.

```{r arapat-axis}
#| cache: true
#| dependson: arapat-graph
nodes <- igraph::V( beetles )$name
lon   <- igraph::V( beetles )$Longitude
lat   <- igraph::V( beetles )$Latitude
xy    <- cbind( x = lon * 111.32 * cos( mean( lat ) * pi / 180 ),
                y = lat * 110.57 )
axis  <- prcomp( xy )
v     <- axis$rotation[, 1] * sign( axis$rotation["y", 1] )
along <- setNames( as.vector( sweep( xy, 2, axis$center ) %*% v ), nodes )
refugium <- ( 27.5 * 110.57 - axis$center["y"] ) / v["y"]
d        <- abs( along - refugium )
```

### Testing each expansion within its component

A small helper runs both tests on one component: the source-sink gradient
test with $d$ as the covariate, and the directional isolation comparison with
separation $|d_i - d_j|$ and forward pairs moving away from the refugium.  The
hypothesis predicts $r(S, d) < 0$ (sources near the refugium), $\Delta R^2 > 0$
and a forward-to-reverse slope ratio below one.

```{r arapat-tests-fn}
#| cache: true
#| dependson: [arapat-graph, arapat-axis]
membership <- igraph::components( beetles )$membership

component_of <- function( site ) {
  same <- membership == membership[nodes == site]
  igraph::induced_subgraph( beetles, nodes[same] )
}

test_expansion <- function( graph ) {
  dk  <- d[igraph::V( graph )$name]
  sep <- abs( outer( dk, dk, "-" ) )
  fwd <- outer( dk, dk, function( di, dj ) dj > di )
  list( gradient    = source_sink_test( graph, x = dk, nperm = 999 ),
        isolation   = ibgd( graph, distance = sep, nperm = 999 ),
        directional = ibgd( graph,
                            mode = "dcGD",
                            distance = sep,
                            forward = fwd ) )
}
```

**Southward expansion (central component).**  Site `93` lies in the central
group:

```{r arapat-south}
#| cache: true
#| dependson: arapat-tests-fn
set.seed( 2013 )
central <- component_of( "93" )
south   <- test_expansion( central )
south
```

Symmetric isolation by graph distance is absent here, but the directional
model recovers it: genetic distance accumulates moving north, toward the
refugium, and not moving south, away from it, the signature of a southward
expansion that averaging the two directions hides.  The source-sink scores
decline away from the refugium as predicted, but the gradient test does not
reject: the component is sparse, and its degree share is large (see the
diagnostics below).

**Northward expansion (northern component).**  Site `9` lies in the
northern group:

```{r arapat-north}
#| cache: true
#| dependson: arapat-tests-fn
set.seed( 2013 )
northern <- component_of( "9" )
north    <- test_expansion( northern )
north
```

Here symmetric isolation by distance is strong, and separate slopes do not
improve on it: distance accumulates at about the same rate in both directions.
With nine sites the source-sink test has little power, so this is weak
evidence about direction either way.

## Is the design adequate? Calibrating the tests

How often the directional tests point somewhere by chance depends on the
sampling design: the number of populations, the individuals in each, and the
loci.  `popgraph_diagnostics()` summarizes the design of the central component
and flags the common problems:

```{r arapat-diagnostics}
#| cache: true
#| dependson: arapat-south
central_sites <- igraph::V( central )$name
central_data  <- peninsula |>
  filter( Population %in% central_sites ) |>
  droplevels()

dg <- central_data |>
  popgraph_diagnostics( graph = central )
dg
```

Each check that has a threshold is marked `✓` or `!`, with a note saying what
a failed check means for the tests.  The same checks are available as a
data frame, and the per-population detail is in `dg$strata`:

```{r arapat-diagnostics-df}
as.data.frame( dg ) |>
  filter( status == "warn" ) |>
  select( check, value, note )
```

With five to ten beetles per site, every site falls below five expected
heterozygotes per locus, and the degree share is large: in such a graph a
population's score depends largely on how many neighbours it has, which is why
the gradient test above could not reject.  The calibrated isolation comparison
is the more reliable test here.

`popgraph_null()` calibrates it.  It simulates data sets with the component's
own sites, sample sizes, loci, alleles and missing genotypes under *symmetric*
migration (Wright-Fisher drift through a symmetric distance kernel, tuned to
the observed $G_{ST}$), rebuilds each Population Graph, and returns the null
distributions of $\Delta R^2$ and $r(S, x)$.  The 95th percentile of the null
$\Delta R^2$ replaces the rule $\Delta R^2 > 0$, and the fraction of null values
at or above the observed one is a one-sided $p$-value.  As for a published
analysis, 999 data sets are simulated:

```{r arapat-null}
#| cache: true
#| dependson: [arapat-south, arapat-diagnostics]
dk  <- d[central_sites]
sep <- abs( outer( dk, dk, "-" ) )
fwd <- outer( dk, dk, function( di, dj ) dj > di )

set.seed( 1 )
calibration <- central_data |>
  popgraph_null( axis = dk,
                 distance = sep,
                 forward = fwd,
                 graph = central,
                 nsim = 999 )
calibration
```

Under symmetric migration with this design, $\Delta R^2 > 0$ arises in a large
fraction of the null data sets, so the observed value alone would mean little;
against the calibrated cutoff, the southward expansion is significant.
Because the null depends on its migration model, check the cutoff's
sensitivity to `Ne`, `ngen` and the kernel (for example a two-dimensional,
great-circle `kernel_distance`).

### Designing a study

- **Individuals per population.**  Each edge is estimated from the variation
  *within* the populations it joins.  The allocation that is optimal for
  estimating differentiation (about $1/\Phi$ individuals per population;
  Falconer 1981, `optimal_sampling()`) is too thin for a Population Graph.
  Aim for roughly five expected heterozygotes per locus in each population
  ($n_i H_S \gtrsim 5$; about 30 individuals at moderate diversity); with ten,
  about half of simulated graphs fragment.
- **Populations.**  Once each is adequately sampled, more populations raise
  the power of the source-sink test.  With fewer than about ten, neither test
  establishes direction from one graph.
- **Loci and coverage.**  More loci raise the power of both tests, and sites
  should span the whole length of the hypothesized direction of flow.
- **Calibrate.**  These guidelines come from a one-dimensional simulation with
  two-allele loci; what carries over is calibrating with `popgraph_null()` for
  your own design.

Starting from the genotypes rather than a graph, `genetic_isolation()` builds
the graph and runs isolation by graph distance in one step, with the axis
given as a column:

```{r arapat-isolation}
#| eval: false
genetic_isolation( peninsula, mode = "IBGD", axis = "Latitude" )
genetic_isolation( peninsula, mode = "dcGD", axis = "Latitude" )
```

## Data quality: information loss

As loci fix, graphs are estimated from fewer informative loci, which inflates
$|\Delta|$ whatever the direction of gene flow.  `locus_subsample_null()`
rebuilds the graph from random subsets of polymorphic loci, to show how much
$|\Delta|$ information loss alone can produce at a given level of polymorphism:

```{r info-loss}
#| eval: false
arapat |>
  locus_subsample_null( k = c( 2, 3, 4, 6 ), nsub = 3 )
```

## Simulating directional gene flow

The `gravity` data come from an individual-based simulation of a directional
stepping stone.  @sec-simulation builds that simulation from scratch with
`make_populations()`, `migration_matrix( model = "stepping_stone_1d_asym" )`
and `simulate_pop()`, and follows the Population Graph and the source-sink
scores through a symmetric burn-in and three forward scenarios.

## Extending the map: a ray-traced source-sink surface {#sec-gravity-3d}

A flat map shows the sign of $S$ by colour, but the shape of the surface, its
ramps, saddles and basins, is easier to see in relief.  `gstudio` does not draw
in three dimensions, and does not need to: `gravity_surface()` returns the
surface and `gravity_field()` the directions, and any renderer can take it from
there.  @fig-gravity-3d does so
with [`rayshader`](https://www.rayshader.com) and `ggplot2`, from the same
beetles as @sec-gravity-map.

![Source-sink surface of *Araptus attenuatus* in relief, with the Population Graph floating above it.  Height and colour are the interpolated $S$ (red, source; blue, sink), with contours every 0.05 and a heavier line at $S = 0$.  Arrows point from source to sink, edges are wider for larger $|\Delta|$, and drop lines mark where each site is.](media/gravity-source-sink-3d.png){#fig-gravity-3d fig-alt="Oblique three-dimensional view of the Baja California peninsula.  The source-sink surface rises in red over the central sites and falls to blue in the south, with a network of labelled sites and arrows above it."}

The code is one documented script,
[gravity-rayshader.R](media/gravity-rayshader.R){download="gravity-rayshader.R"}.
It holds everything from the data to the figure, in eight steps:

1. settings;
2. the data and the `gravity_field`;
3. the surface, resampled to cells that are square on the ground, each
   component on its own;
4. the colours of the map, and a light from the slopes of $S$;
5. the ray-traced render, without OpenGL;
6. the camera, fitted so that any point can be placed on the image;
7. the grid, contours, sites, edges and arrows;
8. the figure, with the network drawn by `ggplot2` so it stays sharp.

Run it from a terminal with `Rscript gravity-rayshader.R`, or with `source()`
in R; give it a file name ending in `.pdf` to keep the network, contours and
labels as vectors.  To use your own data, replace step 2.

::: {.callout-warning title="Before you run it: packages, time and complexity"}
The script is an example and not part of `gstudio`, and it is **not run** when
this book is built; @fig-gravity-3d is a saved image.

**Packages.**  Beyond `gstudio` and the packages it installs, you need:

| Package | Used for |
|---|---|
| `rayshader` | Ray-traced shadows and the 3-D render (also installs `rgl`, `rayvertex`, `rayimage` and `rayrender`) |
| `terra` | The surface as a raster, and its resampling |
| `png` | Reading the render back into R |
| `ggrepel` | Site labels |
| `rnaturalearth`, `rnaturalearthhires` | The land polygons |

The last is not on CRAN; the top of the script has the lines that install them
all.

**Time and memory.**  The figure took about one minute and 9 GB of memory on
an Apple M4 Max laptop.  Work small while choosing a view:
`size = c( 900, 750 )` with `nx <- 300` took 20 seconds and 2.4 GB.

**Complexity.**  An oblique view has costs that a map does not: some ground is
hidden, distances and angles are foreshortened, and values cannot be read off
by position.  Use it to show the shape of a surface, and the flat map of
@sec-gravity-map to read it.
:::

Four things about the picture are not data.  The outer walls are where the
surface was clipped.  The step between the components is meaningless, since
$S$ is not comparable across it.  The height of the network above the surface
is constant, and its arcs only keep it clear of the terrain.  And the surface is
*smoothed*: it spans
-0.49 to 0.34, where the sites' own scores span -0.78 to 0.49.  Direction comes
from each edge and not from the surface, so an arrow may point uphill, as 4 of
the 32 edges do here (2 of them also by the sites' own scores), all with a
small $|\Delta|$ (at most 0.13).

{{< include ../vignettes/children/genetic_gravity_nopipes.Rmd >}}

The *Araptus attenuatus* case study, calibration and data-quality steps:

```{r no-pipes-arapat}
#| eval: false
peninsula <- arapat[arapat$Species == "Peninsula", ]
n_site    <- table( peninsula$Population )
peninsula <- droplevels( peninsula[peninsula$Population %in%
                                     names( n_site )[n_site >= 4], ] )
beetles   <- population_graph( peninsula,
                               stratum = "Population",
                               decorate = TRUE )

mapped <- igraph::induced_subgraph(
  beetles,
  which( parts$csize[parts$membership] > 2 )
)
beetle_field <- gravity_field( mapped )

plot( beetle_field,                          # with the topology
      base = land_map,
      clip_to_base = TRUE,
      grid_n = 400 )
plot( beetle_field,                          # the surface alone
      base = land_map,
      clip_to_base = TRUE,
      grid_n = 400,
      show_graph = FALSE )

gravity_surface( beetle_field,
                 grid_n = 400,
                 clip = land,
                 output = "raster" )

central      <- component_of( "93" )
central_data <- droplevels(
  peninsula[peninsula$Population %in% igraph::V( central )$name, ]
)
dg <- popgraph_diagnostics( central_data,
                            stratum = "Population",
                            graph = central )
warn <- as.data.frame( dg )
warn[warn$status == "warn", c( "check", "value", "note" )]

calibration <- popgraph_null( central_data,
                              stratum = "Population",
                              axis = dk,
                              distance = sep,
                              forward = fwd,
                              graph = central,
                              nsim = 999 )

locus_subsample_null( arapat,
                      stratum = "Population",
                      k = c( 2, 3, 4, 6 ),
                      nsub = 3 )
```
